Spanning multiple European capitals, this coordinated campaign capitalized on the United Kingdom’s landmark decision to designate the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization. Through rallies, human rights exhibitions, and public demonstrations, the diaspora movement actively amplified the internal defiance of domestic Resistance Units , demanding the dismantling of the theocracy, rejecting any return to monarchy, and urging the international community to recognize the democratic roadmap for a secular republic. July 16, 2026 In Rome , thousands of Iranian exiles and prominent international figures gathered for a mass rally demanding an end to executions and the establishment of a democratic republic. National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI) President-elect Maryam Rajavi addressed the crowd via video message, presenting her Ten-Point Plan for a secular, non-nuclear Iran. Speeches by former U.S. Congressman Patrick Kennedy, and former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani highlighted that internal resistance, rather than external intervention, drives true change. The gathering firmly rejected both the current religious dictatorship and the former monarchical regime. Mayor Rudy Giuliani @RudyGiuliani addressing a free Iran conference in Rome, July 16, 2026, examining the roadmap for change, rejecting the mullahs & IRGC, AND the monarchy & SAVAK. He said the MEK is the only viable force able to confront the IRGC and effect change inside Iran. pic.twitter.com/sWj9RmNEKt — Alireza Jafarzadeh (@A_Jafarzadeh) July 18, 2026 July 15, 2026 In Paris , NCRI supporters organized public book stands and photo exhibitions to condemn the recent surge in executions targeting political prisoners and protesters arrested during the January 2026 uprisings . Organizers engaged with the French public to call for international solidarity, emphasizing the Iranian people’s total rejection of all forms of authoritarian rule, whether theocratic or monarchical. July 14, 2026 Coordinated demonstrations swept Northern and Western Europe following the UK’s blacklisting of the IRGC. In Gothenburg , supporters staged a dual rally welcoming the terrorist designation while standing in solidarity with the 129th week of the “ Tuesdays Against Executions ” campaign. Protesters highlighted the critical situation of 1,500 hunger-striking prisoners in Ghezel Hesar Prison, demanding the closure of the Iranian embassy in Sweden. In Copenhagen , Iranians similarly rallied to celebrate the IRGC proscription, calling for the expulsion of regime agents and the closure of the embassy in Denmark. Meanwhile, in Hamburg , supporters of the Iranian Resistance gathered to hold a victory celebration marking the British policy shift against the regime’s primary apparatus of terror. Video #Berlin Car Caravan by PMOI Supporters Welcomes #UK Designation of IRGC as Terrorist Organization – July 13, 2026 #BlacklistIRGC pic.twitter.com/8N58Cm6sdD — Iran Freedom (@4FreedominIran) July 14, 2026 July 13, 2026 The diplomatic offensive centered outside the UK Parliament in London , where activists gathered in Parliament Square to hail the official terrorist designation of the IRGC as a crucial blow to Tehran’s regional destabilization and domestic repression. In Berlin , a high-visibility convoy of vehicles waving Iranian flags and PMOI emblems filed through city streets to celebrate the listing and demand popular sovereignty. Concurrently, supporters in Paris maintained public visibility by hosting another book table and photo exhibition documenting the sacrifices of the domestic uprising. July 11, 2026 Global human rights exhibitions marked the start of the weekly mobilization. In Gothenburg , diaspora members rallied to support internal Resistance Units , advocate for Maryam Rajavi’s Ten-Point Plan, and demand that senior regime officials face international tribunals for crimes against humanity. In Bucharest , an interactive photo exhibition attracted local Romanian citizens who expressed solidarity with the campaign to abolish the death penalty. A similar memorial exhibition in Berlin drew deep support from German locals, including a ten-minute public prayer for Iran’s freedom led by a resident named Mr. Markus. Finally, in Malmö , protesters rallied specifically to denounce the death sentence given to 25-year-old political prisoner Arghavan Fallahi, holding her picture and chanting to demand an immediate halt to her execution. 2-Thousands of Iranians rallied in Rome on July 16, 2026 as @Maryam_Rajavi addressed the Italian Senate and Parliament, voicing support for the democratic alternative, the NCRI, and a democratic republic for Iran. #NCRIAlternative #No2ShahNo2Mullahs #FreeIran10PointPlan pic.twitter.com/0fak6Kzu4m — Iran Freedom (@4FreedominIran) July 17, 2026 This week’s global mobilization underscores an acute existential deadlock for the Iranian regime, demonstrating that Tehran’s reliance on domestic executions and terror has definitively backfired. Rather than stabilizing the state during its fragile leadership transition following the death of Ali Khamenei, escalating repression has instead triggered a synchronized domestic and international backlash that erodes its remaining authority. The UK’s designation of the IRGC as a terrorist entity represents a profound structural failure for the regime’s isolation strategy, stripping away the facade of invincibility that the clerical elite desperately tries to project. Facing an organized domestic underground alongside a unified international diaspora capable of mobilizing across major capitals, the newly installed faction under Mojtaba Khamenei enters power profoundly weakened, proving that state terror can no longer suppress the momentum toward a democratic alternative. People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.’ Photograph: Peter Morgan/REUTERS View image in fullscreen ‘The devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled. People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.’ Photograph: Peter Morgan/REUTERS New York Mamdani releases 170,000 pages of records regarding impact on air quality of 9/11 attacks Documents available through an online portal launched three days before the 25th anniversary of September 11 Victoria Bekiempis Tue 8 Sep 2026 20.40 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration has released more than 170,000 pages of municipal records involving the impact of the September 11 attacks on air quality health, as well as the city’s response. Mamdani announced the documents and an online portal for accessing them on Tuesday. The release comes alongside the settlement of two lawsuits pursued by 9/11 Health Watch, which fought for access to these long-withheld documents. “For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place,” Mamdani said in a statement. “The devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled,” Mamdani also said at a press conference. “People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.” The tranche of documents offers just a fraction of air quality reports on Ground Zero. But they do include an internal memo where New York City weighed possible liability related to air quality. The release of these records comes three days before the 25th anniversary of 9/11 – which killed nearly 3,000 people in New York City, Washington and Pennsylvania. The documents provide further evidence that city officials knew air surrounding the twin towers was toxic – but misled the public into thinking it was safe, officials said. “My colleagues and I who represented Ground Zero and the surrounding communities immediately warned local and federal officials of the health risks posed by toxins in the air at the time,” congressman Jerry Nadler said in a statement. “Our warnings were not heeded, and now we and the public know that city hall, led by former mayor [Rudy] Giuliani, predicted that thousands of responders and community members would face devastating long-term health impacts from these toxins.” New York City council member Gale Brewer voiced similar sentiments. “For 25 years, first responders, survivors, families, and people who lived, worked and went to school in lower Manhattan have lived with the health consequences of 9/11 while critical pieces of the city’s own record – HOW they got sick – remained out of reach,” she said in a statement. The portal, Brewer said, “is a great first step toward giving the public access to that record, one that has been denied them under previous administrations.” Ben Chevat, executive director of 911 Health Watch, thanked Mamdani for “being the mayor, after 25 years, who finally begins to answer the question: ‘What did the city know about the dangers from the toxic cloud at Ground Zero and when did it know it?’ “For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the city council documents showing what the city actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in lower Manhattan and western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as city officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” he said in a statement. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cd94.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Fire and smoke rise at EMCO's ammunition storage facility near Gorni Varpishta in central Bulgaria By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 12 September 2026 Bulgaria is investigating the cause of an overnight fire at an ammunition storage site run by a private defence company. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said the authorities "are not ruling out outside interference" in the incident in central Bulgaria. No-one was injured in the blaze that triggered a series of explosions. EMCO company, whose weapons are used by Ukraine against invading Russian forces, said the fire at its site was sabotage and that human error was "completely ruled out". It did not say who might be responsible. The latest incident follows last month's fire and blasts at another EMCO ammunition warehouse in the area. In a statement, EMCO said the storage facility that was burned this time - near the central village of Gorni Varpishta, some 170km (106 miles) east of the capital Sofia - had not been used for months and was inspected just 20 days ago, when full compliance with all regulations was confirmed. It cited a number of similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, saying that the latest was "no exception to the series of acts of sabotage against the Bulgarian defence industry". "As the EU and Nato member state most severely affected by such actions, Bulgaria must join the collective effort to prevent and neutralise these attacks," EMCO said. The firm is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors allege has already been targeted by Russian agents. This includes a poisoning attempt in 2015 of Gebrev, his son and another company employee - three Russian nationals were later charged in absentia for attempted murder. Bulgaria is a major weapons supplier to Ukraine, as it continues to repel a full-scale Russian invasion launched in 2022. And although Sofia has recently halted state-owned arms supplies to Ukraine, Bulgarian private defence companies continue such transfers. Russia appears to have recently escalated its sabotage campaign across Europe. Last week, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig's airport - a claim denied by Moscow as "absurd". There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia. Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in Literature for her modern twists on Greek mythology and antiquity that have inspired new forms of writing. The 76-year-old – who announced in 2024 that she has Parkinson’s disease – was honoured “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”, the Swedish Academy said. “They’re all crazy,” Carson said of Academy members’ decision to honour her, in an interview with public broadcaster RUV in Iceland where she has lived part of the year since 2008 and has become a citizen. The permanent secretary of the Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, earlier told reporters that she had spoken briefly with Carson to inform her of the prize. “All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.” Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Just in! New Nobel Prize laureate in literature Anne Carson stands surprised in her kitchen in Reykjavík, Iceland. Stay tuned for our exclusive interview with her coming soon. Join us in congratulating our 2026 literature laureate - send your greetings in the comments. pic.twitter.com/vateXOOBMp — The Nobel Prize (@NobelPrize) October 8, 2026 Asked by RUV on a blustery roadside if she thought the Nobel would change her readership, Carson, holding tightly to her cap so it wouldn’t blow away, replied: “I’ll get a sticker on the front of my books.” Carson had at first ignored the Academy’s repeated phone calls. “There were all these phone calls which I kept turning off because ... I just always turn off the phone when it rings,” she said. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Her husband convinced her to call back, she told the Nobel Foundation. A professor of classics with a background in dead languages, literature, anthropology and history, she was described by the New York Times in 2001 as “one of the great pasticheurs”. Her unique contemporary poetry earned her several key literary prizes in the 1990s, including the 1996 Lannan Award and the 1997 Pushcart Prize. A year later, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse – loosely based on the Greek myth of the monster Geryon and Herakles but transformed into a modern tale of a gay love triangle – received widespread praise. ‘Author for our time’ The Academy singled out her 2010 poem Nox , printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her brother who died in 2000, as “an unforgettable work”. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. “Palpable here is a deep sense of loss that works its way up from below. The result is a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother.” It also highlighted her translations from Classical Greek, which “may be regarded as independent works in their own right”. Academy member Steve Sem-Samberg told the Nobel Foundation Carson was “an author for our time”, connecting the contemporary with antiquity. “She uses the myths, the characters, the stories, the fables from that time to put them into a modern context. And the mixture between those two gives an enormous energy to her writing,” he said. “When you’re inside her work, you immediately recognise her voice and her themes. Nobody writes like her,” he told AFP. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. In her own interview with the Nobel Foundation, Carson described her writing as “inadvertant”, coming about while “always trying to do something else”. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the win “an extraordinary achievement and a proud moment for Canada”. Women under-represented In the London Review of Books in 2024, Carson said Parkinson’s had “disintegrated” her handwriting, a “particularly mortifying” symptom. “I used to take pleasure in writing in notebooks, shelves of them, day after day, year after year. Now the upright strokes bend or break or go in all directions, vowels shrink to blobs, slant loses its smooth smart angle, it all looks embarrassing.” Carson had been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years, though some experts said the Academy was unlikely to honour another Canadian so soon after the 2013 prize to short story author Alice Munro. Many literary critics had expected the award to go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the over-representation of Western white men among its picks. There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901. A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced. Advertisement Advertise with NZME. Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman. Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.
